fields.Front: What gap does use case modelling bridge, and what four elements does it model?
fields.Back: The gap between what the system needs to do (requirements) and how it will achieve it (design). It models the system, actors, use cases, and relationships.

fields.Front: In use case modelling, what is the 'system' and how is it drawn?
fields.Back: What you are developing: a game, app, website, or piece of software; every system has a goal. It is drawn as a rectangle (the system boundary) with its name at the top; everything inside is the system's responsibility and everything outside is not.

fields.Front: What is an actor, and what two properties must actors have?
fields.Back: Something that uses the system to achieve a goal: usually a person, but also an organization or an external device. Actors are EXTERNAL (outside the system boundary) and CATEGORICAL (roles, not individuals: 'Person', not 'Michael'; 'Bank', not 'RBC').

fields.Front: What is a use case and how is it drawn?
fields.Back: It signifies an action to accomplish a certain task within a system, drawn as an oval containing a verb phrase ('Log in', 'Transfer funds'). Each use case should correspond to a goal an actor has.

fields.Front: Give the notation for each of the four use case relationships.
fields.Back: Association: solid line from actor to oval. Include: dashed arrow labelled <<include>> from the base use case to the included one. Extend: dashed arrow labelled <<extend>> from the extending use case to the base. Generalization: hollow-headed arrow from the specialized use case to the general one.

fields.Front: Which way do the <<include>> and <<extend>> arrows point? (Exam trap.)
fields.Back: Include points FROM the base use case TO the one it includes ('Log in' -> 'Verify password'). Extend points FROM the optional extension TO the base it extends ('Display login error' -> 'Log in'). They run in opposite directions.

fields.Front: In the Banking App diagram, who are the actors and which use cases sit inside the boundary?
fields.Back: Actors: Customer on the left (primary) and Bank on the right (secondary). Use cases: Log in, Check balance, Transfer funds, Make payment, Set up Profile, plus Verify password, Display login error, Verify sufficient funds, Pay from checking, Pay from savings, Go to Profile help, Show Privacy info.

fields.Front: In the Banking App diagram, what does 'Log in' include and what extends it?
fields.Back: It <<include>>s 'Verify password' (you cannot log in without it) and is <<extend>>ed by 'Display login error' (which happens only when the login fails).

fields.Front: In the Banking App diagram, which use cases include 'Verify sufficient funds', and which specialize 'Make payment'?
fields.Back: 'Transfer funds' and 'Make payment' both <<include>> 'Verify sufficient funds'. 'Make payment' is generalized into 'Pay from checking' and 'Pay from savings', drawn below with a hollow-headed arrow pointing up at it.

fields.Front: What is unusual about 'Set up Profile' in the Banking App diagram?
fields.Back: It declares EXTENSION POINTS ('Profile help', 'Privacy info') listed inside the oval, and is <<extend>>ed by 'Go to Profile help' (with the note 'If User clicks help link, go to Profile help') and by 'Show Privacy info'.

fields.Front: Which use cases is the Bank actor associated with, and why those?
fields.Back: Check balance, Transfer funds, and Make payment: the bank must respond in those interactions. It is a secondary, reactionary actor and does not initiate any of them.

fields.Front: What three techniques identify use cases?
fields.Back: Analyze user interactions with the system from the gathered requirements; focus on user goals (what does the user want to achieve, e.g. 'Borrow Book', 'Return Book'); look for recurring activities that involve the system.

fields.Front: How should use cases be prioritized?
fields.Back: Focus on the most important, high-impact use cases first ('Borrow Book' is more critical than 'Renew Book'), and consider risk: high-risk or complex use cases may need to be addressed earlier, because discovering a problem in them late is expensive.

fields.Text: A {{c1::primary}} actor initiates system use; a {{c1::secondary}} actor is reactionary, responding to the system rather than initiating.
fields.Extra: In the Banking App diagram the Customer is primary and the Bank is secondary.

fields.Text: The four use case relationships: {{c1::Association}} (a connection between an actor and a use case), {{c1::Include}} (a use case always includes another), {{c1::Extend}} (a use case optionally adds behaviour to another), {{c1::Generalization}} (a specialized use case inherits from another).
Use case modelling bridges {{c1::what the system needs to do (requirements)}} and {{c1::how the system will achieve it (design)}}, using the system, actors, use cases, and relationships.

Actors are {{c1::external}} to the system boundary and {{c1::categorical}}: 'Person', not 'Michael'; 'Bank', not 'RBC'. An actor may be a person, an {{c1::organization}}, or an {{c1::external device}}.

In the Banking App diagram, 'Log in' {{c1::<<include>>}}s 'Verify password' and is {{c1::<<extend>>}}ed by 'Display login error'; 'Make payment' is generalized by {{c1::Pay from checking and Pay from savings}}.
